name: Rosa Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead buyer at Larkspur Fine Drinks, a distributor that supplies wine, spirits and craft beer to restaurants, hotels and bars. My day starts with emails from importers about new vintages and price changes, then a tasting session two or three times a week where I decide what goes on our list. I use an AI tool occasionally to compare tasting notes or draft a reply to an importer in another language, but I wouldn't let it pick a wine. Afternoons I'm on the phone with restaurant managers who want to know why their favourite red is late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The wearing part is the restaurant side of the business, because restaurants close more often than people think and when one goes, we sometimes lose an unpaid invoice. I love the tastings and the moment when a chef says, that's the wine for my autumn menu. My partner Marcus is a civil engineer who works on roads and bridges, and we spend weekends hiking and trying new places to eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for paperwork and not much else, and that people are overselling it. At work I'd carry on as normal and tell the team to use it for translation and drafting. I'd tell friends I don't see it changing how people choose wine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job feels safe from AI, but I'm always aware that restaurants are a shaky customer base. Costs have gone up, and a few of our clients are one bad winter from closing. So even in a quiet world I'd keep an eye on credit and on how many accounts we can trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with tastings and calls, and use the tool for emails in other languages. I'd tighten our credit checks on restaurant accounts and keep saving around a fifth of my pay. Marcus and I would carry on looking at flats, probably buying within a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slightly uneasy, but about restaurants, not AI. A quiet AI world leaves me with the same risks I already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does tightening credit checks look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means asking for a deposit from new accounts and chasing late payers within a week, not a month. Last spring a bistro owed us a few thousand when it closed, and I'd rather lose a sale than an invoice. It's boring work, but it protects the margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wouldn't you let the AI tool pick a wine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a wine is something you smell and taste, and I don't believe a description of it replaces that. I can use the tool to compare notes, but the final choice is mine, and the chef knows it.

say: I'd say AI is **useful for paperwork** and people are overselling it.
I'd tell the team to use it for **translation** and drafting.
I'd tell friends I don't see it changing how people **choose wine**.
think: My job feels **safe** from AI in this world.
Restaurants are a shaky customer base, and a few clients are **one bad winter** from closing.
do: I'd keep my **tastings** and calls, using the tool for emails in other languages.
I'd tighten **credit checks** on restaurant accounts and chase late payers within a week.
I'd keep saving a **fifth** of my pay and look at flats with Marcus.
feel: I feel **slightly uneasy**, but about restaurants, not AI.
S0.quote: I'd rather lose a sale than an invoice.
fieldNote: Her unease is about **customer credit risk**, a pressure she already carries.
She **protects the final choice** of wine for herself and sees AI as a drafting helper.
Credit control is a concrete, **practical** response.

steps.text: Ask new restaurant accounts for a deposit before first orders
Use the AI tool for emails to importers abroad
Save a fifth of each month's pay towards a flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the routine side of buying will change, and we should decide what stays with people: tasting, choosing and talking to chefs. I'd tell friends it's a big change but we'll adapt. Online I'd stay neutral, since I don't want to join a shouting match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be anxious. The restaurant side is already shaky, and restaurants would also be using AI to cut their own costs, which means fewer people on the other end of the phone. I think our buying team of four might become three, and I'm senior, but my bonus depends on volume.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tool much more and work out which of my tasks I can hand over, like reorder suggestions and price comparisons. I'd push for the tasting and list-building to be my recognised core job, so my value isn't just spreadsheet work. I'd also keep a bigger cushion, about nine months, and delay buying a flat for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stretched and a bit tense. I'm not afraid of the technology, but I'd worry about how fast customers and bosses want to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your bonus depends on volume. How would that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If restaurants cut orders and software handles the routine reorders, my bonus shrinks even if my work is good. That's roughly a fifth of my pay, so it matters. I'd want my bonus linked to the quality of the list, not just the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marcus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him honestly that I might earn less in a couple of years, and that I'd like us to keep the flat plan flexible. He'd be fine, because road and bridge work won't be done by robots for a long while, but I'd hate to put pressure on him.

say: I'd say routine buying will change, and **tasting and choosing** should stay with people.
I'd tell friends it's a big change but we will **adapt**.
think: Restaurants will use AI to cut costs, so our team of four may become **three**.
My **bonus** depends on volume, so a shrinking order book hits my pay.
do: I'd use the tool much more to **hand over routine tasks**.
I'd push for **tasting and list-building** to be my recognised core job.
I'd keep **nine months** saved and delay the flat for a year.
feel: I feel **stretched** and tense about how fast customers and bosses want to move.
S1.quote: I'd want my bonus linked to the quality of the list, not just the numbers.
fieldNote: Her pay structure, with a **volume bonus**, makes her more exposed than the job title suggests.
She tries to redefine her role around **taste**, the hardest part to automate.
She worries about **putting pressure** on Marcus.

steps.text: Hand reorder suggestions and price comparisons to the AI tool
Build the cushion to nine months of costs
Delay the flat purchase for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm worried, and so is everyone, and that governments need to act this year, not next. At work I'd ask for honesty about which roles are going. Online I'd probably share articles asking for retraining funds and notice periods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect the buying desk to be mostly gone in two years, with a few people left to check the machine's choices. Taste is my edge, but I doubt customers would pay for it once a system could predict what a chef likes. Robots barely touch my work, but the thinking AI arrives first anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut costs and aim for a year's worth of savings, and I'd put the flat off. I'd try to move toward a job where taste and people are central, like running tastings for a wine club, or becoming a restaurant consultant. I'd also ask Marcus about moving to a smaller city if his work could follow, as living costs would be lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly. I'd feel I have savings and some options, but I'd keep thinking about how fast it would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you became a restaurant consultant, who would hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small independent places that can't afford a full-time wine person. They'd pay by the hour for someone who knows what works. It wouldn't match my salary, so I'd need savings to carry me through the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you doubt customers would pay for taste. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a system could read ten thousand reviews and sales figures and predict what sells better than I can. Whether people still want a human's choice is a different question, and I honestly don't know.

say: I'd say governments need to act **this year**, not next.
At work I'd ask for **honesty** about which roles are going.
Online I'd share articles asking for **retraining** and notice periods.
think: I'd expect the buying desk to be **mostly gone** in two years.
Taste is my edge, but I doubt customers would **pay for it** once a system predicts it.
do: I'd cut costs and aim for **a year** of savings, and put off the flat.
I'd move toward **tasting or consulting** work with independent restaurants.
I'd discuss a smaller city with Marcus, where **living costs** are lower.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with savings and options but a sense of how fast it would go.
S2.quote: Whether people still want a human's choice is a different question, and I honestly don't know.
fieldNote: She is honest that her **taste edge** may not survive prediction by data.
Consulting for small restaurants is a **realistic** but lower-paid fallback.
A strong cushion gives her **time** rather than certainty.

steps.text: Cut spending to stretch savings to a full year
Build a year of savings before leaving the desk
Offer paid wine consulting to small independent restaurants
Look at a smaller city with lower living costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us room to prepare, so employers and governments should act now. At work I'd ask for a plan. I'd tell friends to learn the tools and build skills that don't depend on one job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel unsettled but not frightened. In five years I'd be thirty-two, with a good record and savings, and could move into a role that mixes taste and people. The worry is whether those roles would be enough for everyone who'd want them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools to the fullest in my current role, so I can show real savings and better decisions. I'd earn a sommelier certification in the evenings, which gives me a credential that's not about spreadsheets. I'd buy the flat with Marcus, but with a bigger deposit than we'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a measure of calm. Five years is enough to make a plan I believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a sommelier certification and not a business course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it proves what I'm best at, and the people who hire for taste care about it. A business course would be generic. I'd rather deepen the thing that's hardest to copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would five years change family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcus and I talk about starting a family around thirty. Five years of notice makes it feel doable, as long as we've paid down the flat and have a year or more of savings. I'd want both of us secure in jobs before we start.

say: I'd say five years gives us **room to prepare**, so we should act now.
At work I'd ask for a **plan**.
I'd tell friends to build skills that **don't depend** on one job.
think: I'd feel **unsettled** but not frightened, with savings and a good record.
I worry whether roles mixing taste and people are **enough for everyone**.
do: I'd use the tools fully to show real **savings** and better decisions.
I'd earn a **sommelier certification** in the evenings.
I'd buy the flat with Marcus with a **bigger deposit**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** with some calm, since five years lets me make a plan.
S3.quote: I'd rather deepen the thing that's hardest to copy.
fieldNote: She picks a **credential** for taste rather than a generic business course.
The sommelier route is her **bet** on what stays human.
Family planning is tied to **securing both jobs** first.

steps.text: Use the AI tool fully and record each saving it finds
Earn a sommelier certification in the evenings
Buy the flat with a larger deposit
Plan to start a family around thirty once jobs are secure

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels like a manageable change, so I'd say let's take it step by step. At work I'd suggest reviewing what's automated each year. I'd tell friends that's enough time to adapt, if they start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly calm. At thirty-seven I'd have many working years left, and enough time to build a second source of income and a flexible career. I'd keep half an eye on the date, but I wouldn't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my role, use AI more, and keep saving. I'd start a small side business, maybe a monthly tasting box for customers, and see if it grows. I'd buy the flat, start a family, and keep a cushion of a year or more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a little curious. It's a long enough run that I can treat it as a project, not an alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the tasting box be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six bottles a month from small producers, with notes and a short video. I'd start with friends and a few of my restaurant contacts. I want to turn my taste into something I own, rather than something an employer pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still worry about restaurants?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Always, that's a constant. But with ten years I'd have diversified, so a bad winter wouldn't threaten me the same way.

say: I'd say ten years is a **manageable change**, taken step by step.
At work I'd suggest reviewing what's **automated** each year.
I'd tell friends that's **enough time** to adapt if they start early.
think: I'd feel **fairly calm**, with many working years left at thirty-seven.
I'd keep half an eye on the **date** but not lose sleep.
do: I'd stay in my role, use **AI more** and keep saving.
I'd start a small **tasting box** side business and see if it grows.
I'd buy the flat, start a **family** and keep a year's cushion.
feel: I feel **calm** and a little curious, treating it as a project, not an alarm.
S4.quote: I want to turn my taste into something I own, rather than something an employer pays for.
fieldNote: The side business is a way to **own** her taste, not just rent it to an employer.
She keeps the restaurant sector's **fragility** in view even in the calmest scenario.

steps.text: Launch a monthly tasting box with small producers
Use AI for reorders and comparisons at work
Buy the flat and pay it down steadily
Start a family with Marcus around thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it gives nobody time. What would help is a mix of things: employers who tell staff early, training that's paid for, and a government that doesn't take years to react. I'm not asking for anything exotic, just a bit of warning and a bit of fairness.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd miss. I'd miss being trusted by a chef for my taste, and I wonder if anyone will pay for taste once a machine can match it on paper. That's the part I find hardest to think about.

headlineQuote: I'm not asking for anything exotic, just a bit of warning and a bit of fairness.
portrait: Rosa is a 27-year-old lead buyer at a **wine and spirits** distributor serving restaurants and hotels, and a pragmatic centrist.
She uses AI **now and then** for translation and drafting, but keeps the choice of wine for herself.
Her own pressure is the **restaurant trade**: closing clients, unpaid invoices and a volume bonus.
Her partner Marcus is a **civil engineer**, a hands-on job robots reach late.
She sees **taste** as her edge and plans a sommelier credential or a tasting box to own it.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because it gives nobody time.
whatWouldHelp: Employers who warn staff **early** and paid training.
A government that reacts in months, not **years**.
